name: SHU-9119

card.summary: Lab melanocortin antagonist used in rodent appetite research; no human studies and no approved use.

quick.overview:
SHU-9119 is a research peptide that blocks melanocortin receptors. Scientists have used it in rats to study appetite, body weight and insulin action.

It has no approved use and no human trials were found.
quick.mechanism: It antagonizes melanocortin receptors (MC3R and MC4R) in the brain, opposing the signal of alpha-MSH.
quick.risks: No human safety data exist; in animals, blocking this pathway increased feeding.

lead: SHU-9119 (also written SHU9119) is a synthetic cyclic peptide that blocks melanocortin receptors and is used in laboratories as a tool for studying appetite, body weight and fat distribution. It is relevant to body composition because the melanocortin system it blocks is one of the brain pathways that tells animals to eat less and keep body fat down, so animal experiments using it have helped explain how appetite and abdominal fat are regulated.[1][2]

In rat and mouse experiments it is infused into the brain, where it opposes the natural activating hormone alpha-MSH and the synthetic agonist MTII, and it increases feeding and body weight.[2][3][4] A 2001 rat study reported that week-long infusions into the third cerebral ventricle changed insulin action and the distribution of body fat in the opposite direction from alpha-MSH, which reduced intra-abdominal fat.[1]

It is not an approved drug and no human clinical studies were found. It remains a preclinical research peptide, and the structure of its complex with the human melanocortin 4 receptor has been used to design new receptor ligands.[5]

chain: Blocks melanocortin 3 and 4 receptors in the brain
In animals: more eating, weight gain and altered fat distribution
angle.text: SHU-9119 is a laboratory tool whose appearance-relevant interest is mechanistic: by blocking the melanocortin pathway it shows how that pathway keeps appetite and abdominal fat in check, the opposite of what agonist peptides do. Its effects in animals are increased feeding and weight gain, not leanness.

paras: The melanocortin system is a set of five receptors, MC1R to MC5R, and their peptide ligands. In the brain, neurons that make the activating peptide alpha-MSH signal through MC3R and MC4R to reduce appetite, while neurons that make agouti-related peptide (AgRP) block those receptors and stimulate eating.[12] AgRP was identified by two research teams in 1997 through its similarity to agouti signalling peptide, a skin protein that controls coat colour; it competes with alpha-MSH at MC3R and MC4R and also acts as an inverse agonist, and its levels rise during fasting.[12]

SHU9119 is a synthetic antagonist at these receptors, so it has been used pharmacologically to ask what happens when melanocortin signalling in the brain is blocked. That is the context for the infusion studies below, in which blocking the receptors increased feeding and shifted body fat.[1][2][3]

SHU-9119 is a cyclic, lactam-bridged melanotropin analogue, Ac-Nle4-c[Asp5-His6-DNal(2')7-Arg8-Trp9-Lys10]-NH2, belonging to the same family of cyclic alpha-MSH analogues as the agonist MT-II.[5][6] Reviews of melanocortin ligand design describe alpha-MSH, MT-II and SHU-9119 as potent, stable analogues that are not very selective between receptor subtypes.[8]

It acts as an antagonist at the MC3 and MC4 receptors and has been shown, in modified forms, to have agonist activity at MC5R; swapping the histidine at position 6 for proline gave a potent hMC5R agonist while retaining antagonism at hMC3R and hMC4R.[7] Structure-activity work has made many lactam derivatives of MT-II and SHU-9119 to tune selectivity at MC3R, MC4R and MC5R.[6][7] A 2021 cocrystal structure of SHU-9119 bound to human MC4R was used to design more selective cyclic peptides, and a 2026 paper described macrocyclic analogues based on MT-II and SHU-9119.[5][9]

A 1997 Nature study identified cyclic melanocortin analogues that were potent agonists or antagonists of the MC3 and MC4 receptors. The agonist MTII inhibited feeding in four mouse models of hyperphagia, SHU9119 blocked that effect, and SHU9119 alone increased nocturnal feeding and fasting-induced feeding, supporting the view that melanocortin neurons exert a tonic inhibition of feeding and offering an explanation for the agouti obesity syndrome in mice.[2]

A 1998 rat study delivered MTII and SHU9119 to the fourth ventricle of the brain and found that the agonist reduced food intake and body weight while the antagonist produced dose-related increases in both; the weight changes appeared secondary to changes in feeding.[3] A 2001 Journal of Clinical Investigation study infused alpha-MSH or SHU9119 into the third ventricle of conscious rats for a week while holding food intake constant: alpha-MSH decreased intra-abdominal fat and enhanced insulin action on glucose uptake and production, and SHU9119 had the opposite effects.[1]

A 2001 rat study found that SHU9119 given into the brain reversed anorexia in tumor-bearing rats, raising food intake from about 71 to 110 percent of baseline, while it did not increase intake in control rats pair-fed to the tumor-bearing animals; the authors concluded that increased central melanocortin signalling contributes to cancer anorexia.[4] A 2023 rat study found that 7 days of MC4R blockade with SHU-9119 increased calorie intake and body weight more in offspring of obese parents than of lean parents and that it lowered blood pressure more in some groups.[10]

The melanocortin system also underlies agonist peptides that have drawn interest for tanning, appetite and sexual function, such as melanotan II. Wikipedia's MC4R article lists afamelanotide, bremelanotide, melanotan II and setmelanotide as synthetic agonists, with agouti-related peptide, agouti signalling peptide and SHU9119 as antagonists; setmelanotide is FDA-approved for chronic weight management in people with certain POMC-related variants and bremelanotide was approved in 2019 for low sexual desire in premenopausal women.[11] In 1998 two groups reported MC4R frameshift mutations in families with severe early-onset obesity, and Wikipedia estimates MC4R variants in about 1 to 2.5 percent of people with obesity.[11]
No studies found. Research on SHU-9119 consists of cell-based pharmacology and animal studies in rats and mice.[1][2][3][4][10]

timeline.event: Nature study shows MTII and SHU9119 modulate feeding in mice and links melanocortin antagonism to the agouti obesity syndrome.[2]
Rat studies report effects of SHU9119 on insulin action and fat distribution and on cancer anorexia.[1][4]
Structure-based ligand design uses the SHU-9119-hMC4R cocrystal structure.[5]
